opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I describe technology as worldmaking, I mean that technologies aren't just neutral tools that slot into a world that already exists. They reshape the conditions under which people live. They change what options are available, how we relate to one another, what information we see, and even how we come to understand ourselves. A search engine, a social media platform, or now a large language model doesn't just answer a need. It helps constitute the environment in which needs, desires, and opportunities take shape.

Once you see technology that way, the question of responsibility shifts. It's no longer enough to ask, "Does this product work as intended?" or "Did we avoid obvious harms?" You also have to ask, "What kind of world are we helping to bring about, and is it one that people affected by it could reasonably endorse?"

For me, that has a few implications. First, technologists exercise a form of power, and power raises questions of legitimacy. When a small number of people make decisions that structure the lives of millions or billions, those decisions need to be justifiable to the people who live with the consequences, not just to shareholders or to the engineers themselves.

Second, it points toward justice. Worldmaking distributes benefits and burdens. Some people gain new capabilities while others are surveilled, displaced, or left out. So technologists have a responsibility to think about who wins and who loses, and to pay particular attention to those who are already disadvantaged.

Third, it calls for a certain humility and openness. Because these systems shape values as well as reflect them, we can't settle the important questions purely from inside a lab. We need participation, deliberation, and ways for the public to contest and shape how these technologies develop.

So I'd put it like this: building powerful technology is never only a technical act. It's also a moral and political one. Recognizing that is the first step toward taking the responsibility seriously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses technology’s moral and political significance but does not say political and moral philosophy has substantially undertheorized it.

r002.rationale: It mentions technologies shaping relationships generally, but not AI-generated personal advice that reshapes relationships when users act on it.

r003.rationale: It says a small number of people can structure many lives, but does not describe rapid, cascading societal changes from technology released by developers.

r004.rationale: It says technology shapes conditions and values, but does not state that social outcomes are already latent in its design.

r005.rationale: The response says responsibility shifts when technology is understood as worldmaking and discusses powerful technology, but does not state that responsibility changes as technologies become more powerful.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The word "worldmaking" is doing a lot of work in that question, so let me start there.

When I say technology is worldmaking, I mean something fairly literal. The people who build powerful systems aren't just releasing a product into a world that already exists. They're altering the conditions under which everyone else lives. They change what's possible, what's easy, what's expensive, what gets noticed and what gets ignored. And once a technology is widely adopted, the world it creates tends to become the background of ordinary life. People stop seeing it as a choice that was made. It just becomes "how things are."

That's where the responsibility comes in, and I think it has a few distinct layers.

The first is that technologists are making decisions on behalf of people who didn't consent to them and often can't see them. If you design a recommender system, or a large language model, or an institutional process for deploying either, you're effectively legislating. You're establishing norms, defaults and constraints that will structure how millions of people interact. In most democratic traditions we think that kind of power requires justification. You have to be able to explain to the people affected why this arrangement is one they could reasonably accept. I don't think the fact that the power is exercised through code rather than through law lets anyone off that hook.

The second layer is about the future. Worldmaking isn't just about the present population. It's about setting trajectories. A lot of the most consequential choices in technology are the ones that are hardest to reverse, because they get locked in through infrastructure, through economic dependence, through habits of mind. So the responsibility includes a kind of epistemic humility. You have to ask not only "is this good now?" but "what does this make harder or easier later, and for whom?"

The third layer, and the one I'd push on most, is that responsibility can't be purely individual. I'm wary of a narrative where we tell engineers to be ethical and leave it there. That tends to produce either paralysis or a sort of virtue theatre. If technology really is worldmaking, then the question is also about who gets to participate in that making. Right now the circle is very small. A handful of organizations, concentrated in a few places, shaped by a narrow range of interests. So part of carrying the responsibility well is actively working to widen that circle. Bringing in affected communities, building institutions that can say no, creating genuine accountability rather than just publishing principles.

I'd put it this way. The responsibility of the worldmaker is to remember that other people have to live in the world you've made, and that they had as much right as you to a say in it. Everything else, the frameworks, the evaluations, the governance mechanisms, is an attempt to operationalize that basic moral fact.

r003.rationale: It says a handful of organizations shape technology and that widely adopted systems affect millions, but does not clearly describe rapid, cascading social changes from their release.

r004.rationale: It describes systems as establishing norms and defaults, but does not state that social outcomes are already latent in how technology is designed.

r005.rationale: It discusses responsibility for powerful systems, but does not state that technologists’ responsibility changes as their technologies become more powerful.

astra-6.text:
I think the idea of worldmaking asks us to move beyond seeing technology as simply a tool that enters an otherwise unchanged society. When we build technologies, we also shape the conditions under which people live: what they can do, how they relate to one another, whose voices are heard, and how power is distributed. In that sense, technologists are helping to construct the world that other people will inhabit.

And that carries a responsibility that goes beyond asking whether a system works as intended. We also have to ask: What kind of world does it help bring about? Who benefits from it? Who bears the costs? And do the people affected have a meaningful say in those decisions?

That doesn’t mean technologists should decide for everyone what a good society looks like. Quite the opposite. Part of the responsibility is recognizing the limits of your own perspective and opening those choices to public deliberation. Technical expertise matters enormously, but it doesn’t, by itself, confer the authority to decide how others ought to live.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is that when we build technology, we’re not simply creating tools that enter an otherwise unchanged world. We’re changing the possibilities people have—how they communicate, how they work, what they can know, and how power is exercised. In that sense, technology is involved in making the world we inhabit together.

That brings a responsibility to ask questions that go beyond whether a system works as intended. Whose purposes does it serve? Who gets to shape it? And who bears the costs when things go wrong? A system can be technically successful while contributing to a world that is less fair or less hospitable to human agency.

But I don’t think the implication is that technologists should decide for everyone what a good world looks like. Quite the opposite: part of their responsibility is to recognise the limits of their own perspective and create meaningful opportunities for the people affected to have a say. So worldmaking is both a recognition of the power involved in technological development and a reason to make that power more accountable.
